book_title: Nine Yard Sarees: A Short Story Cycle
subject_line: The scattered family in Nine Yard Sarees
email_body:
Dear Prasanthi,

Nine Yard Sarees follows several generations of a Tamil Brahmin family dispersed across Singapore, Australia and the United States, and I was struck by your choice of a short story cycle rather than a single novel to hold them together.

I would love to ask how you decided which family members got their own stories, and what the cycle form let you do with distance between them.

The Author Ledger is an independent project featuring short Author Spotlights. Each portrait comes from a few written questions you can answer at your own pace, and the full text is shared with you for review before publication.

Would you be open to taking part? No pressure either way.

Best regards,
The Author Ledger
hook_note: Debut short story cycle (Ethos Books, 2023) about a Tamil Brahmin family across Singapore, Australia and USA; won SLP 2024 English Fiction (NTU news, Sing Lit Station). No email found in search results.

subject_line: Lockdown poems in Anatomy of a Wave
email_body:
Dear Shu Hoong,

In your Tatler Asia interview you described the worst lockdowns as becoming a kind of writing residency, and many of the poems from that time ended up in Anatomy of a Wave, which brought you a third Singapore Literature Prize.

I would like to ask what that enforced stillness changed in how you wrote, and whether the wave of the title came before or after those poems.

book_title: The Campbell Gardens Ladies' Swimming Class
subject_line: Learning to swim at Campbell Gardens
email_body:
Dear Vrushali,

The Campbell Gardens Ladies' Swimming Class, winner of the 2023 Epigram Books Fiction Prize, puts a group of Indian women in a Singapore condominium into the pool to learn to swim. It is a setting I have not met in fiction before.

I would love to ask where the swimming class came from, and how your life as a dentist living in Singapore fed into the novel.

book_title: Gus: The Life and Opinions of the Last Raffles' Banded Langur
subject_line: Gus and the way back to Bukit Timah
email_body:
Dear Jon,

Gus, your talking langur who wants to find his way home to the jungles of Bukit Timah Nature Reserve, is an unusual narrator for the end of the world.

I would like to ask why you gave this story to the last Raffles' banded langur, and how the voice of Gus changed from your short stories in We Rose Up Slowly.

subject_line: Doris's last request in Patrick Zhou
email_body:
Dear Ally,

The Disappearance of Patrick Zhou opens on a striking request: Doris, in her last lucid moments, asks her granddaughter Layla to find out what happened to an uncle who vanished on his way to a conference.

As a poet as well as a novelist, how did you approach a mystery built around family memory, and did you know what had happened to Patrick before you started writing?

book_title: We Do Not Make Love Here
subject_line: Four voices in We Do Not Make Love Here
email_body:
Dear Nisha,

We Do Not Make Love Here tells its family saga through four ordinary Indian Singaporeans, and I was interested to learn it began as a manuscript shortlisted for the 2022 Epigram Books Fiction Prize before reaching the Singapore Literature Prize shortlist in two categories.

I would like to ask how you chose those four perspectives, and whether your years as a teacher shaped the kind of ordinary lives you wanted to write about.

subject_line: 44 old poems and 44 new in ownself say ownself
email_body:
Dear Joshua,

ownself say ownself has a structure I keep thinking about: 44 poems salvaged from your earlier books set beside 44 new translations, performance pieces and formal experiments. It reads like a poet arguing with his own back catalogue.

I would love to ask how you chose what to salvage, and what putting the old poems next to the new ones showed you about your own writing since sonnets from the singlish.

subject_line: We Make Spaces Divine, from page to stage
email_body:
Dear Pooja,

We Make Spaces Divine, your 2021 Math Paper Press collection of poems walking through cities in bodies that don't belong, found a second life at the Esplanade during Kalaa Utsavam 2025, performed alongside Shivram Gopinath.

I would like to ask what changed when the poems moved from the page into a shared performance, and whether staging them altered how you hear the collection now.
